### Technique 1: Offloading - Summarization and Reference Management

Offloading is the practice of summarizing information and storing full data in external references, allowing the agent to access detailed information only when needed. When an AI agent makes a tool call—for example, querying a database or calling an external API—it receives a response that could be quite large. Rather than dumping the entire response into the context window, offloading involves summarizing the key information and providing a reference that the agent can use to retrieve the full data if necessary.

A practical example of this approach comes from Manus AI, a research organization working on advanced AI agents. When their agent makes a tool call and receives a response, they don’t include the entire response in the context. Instead, they provide a concise summary of the response and store the full tool call result in a file or database with a reference pointer. If the agent later determines that it needs more detailed information from that tool call, it can reference the stored data without consuming additional context tokens in the main conversation. This approach mirrors how humans work—we don’t memorize every detail of every conversation, but we keep notes and references we can consult when needed.

Summary: 
According to the article, Manus AI uses a technique called 'offloading' to manage context and save tokens. When their agent receives a large response from a tool call (e.g., a database query), they do not include the entire response in the main conversation's context window. Instead, they summarize the key information for the agent and store the full data in an external reference, such as a file or database. The agent is then provided with a pointer or reference to this stored data, which it can access if it needs more detailed information later. This method allows the agent to function with a leaner, high-signal context while still having access to complete data when necessary.

Evidence in page: 
### Design Around the KV-Cache

If I had to choose just one metric, I'd argue that the KV-cache hit rate is the single most important metric for a production-stage AI agent. It directly affects both latency and cost. To understand why, let's look at how a typical agent operates:

After receiving a user input, the agent proceeds through a chain of tool uses to complete the task. In each iteration, the model selects an action from a predefined action space based on the current context. That action is then executed in the environment (e.g., Manus's virtual machine sandbox) to produce an observation. The action and observation are appended to the context, forming the input for the next iteration. This loop continues until the task is complete.

As you can imagine, the context grows with every step, while the output—usually a structured function call—remains relatively short. This makes the ratio between prefilling and decoding highly skewed in agents compared to chatbots. In Manus, for example, the average input-to-output token ratio is around 100:1.

Fortunately, contexts with identical prefixes can take advantage of KV-cache, which drastically reduces time-to-first-token (TTFT) and inference cost—whether you're using a self-hosted model or calling an inference API. And we're not talking about small savings: with Claude Sonnet, for instance, cached input tokens cost 0.30 USD/MTok, while uncached ones cost 3 USD/MTok—a 10x difference.

From a context engineering perspective, improving KV-cache hit rate involves a few key practices:

1.Keep your prompt prefix stable. Due to the autoregressive nature of LLMs, even a single-token difference can invalidate the cache from that token onward. A common mistake is including a timestamp—especially one precise to the second—at the beginning of the system prompt. Sure, it lets the model tell you the current time, but it also kills your cache hit rate.

2.Make your context append-only. Avoid modifying previous actions or observations. Ensure your serialization is deterministic. Many programming languages and libraries don't guarantee stable key ordering when serializing JSON objects, which can silently break the cache.

3.Mark cache breakpoints explicitly when needed. Some model providers or inference frameworks don't support automatic incremental prefix caching, and instead require manual insertion of cache breakpoints in the context. When assigning these, account for potential cache expiration and at minimum, ensure the breakpoint includes the end of the system prompt.

Additionally, if you're self-hosting models using frameworks like vLLM, make sure prefix/prompt caching is enabled, and that you're using techniques like session IDs to route requests consistently across distributed workers.

### Mask, Don't Remove

As your agent takes on more capabilities, its action space naturally grows more complex—in plain terms, the number of tools explodes. The recent popularity of MCP only adds fuel to the fire. If you allow user-configurable tools, trust me: someone will inevitably plug hundreds of mysterious tools into your carefully curated action space. As a result, the model is more likely to select the wrong action or take an inefficient path. In short, your heavily armed agent gets dumber.

A natural reaction is to design a dynamic action space—perhaps loading tools on demand using something RAG-like. We tried that in Manus too. But our experiments suggest a clear rule: unless absolutely necessary, avoid dynamically adding or removing tools mid-iteration. There are two main reasons for this:

1.In most LLMs, tool definitions live near the front of the context after serialization, typically before or after the system prompt. So any change will invalidate the KV-cache for all subsequent actions and observations.

2.When previous actions and observations still refer to tools that are no longer defined in the current context, the model gets confused. Without constrained decoding, this often leads to schema violations or hallucinated actions.

To solve this while still improving action selection, Manus uses a context-aware state machine to manage tool availability. Rather than removing tools, it masks the token logits during decoding to prevent (or enforce) the selection of certain actions based on the current context.

### Use the File System as Context

Modern frontier LLMs now offer context windows of 128K tokens or more. But in real-world agentic scenarios, that's often not enough, and sometimes even a liability. There are three common pain points:

1.Observations can be huge, especially when agents interact with unstructured data like web pages or PDFs. It's easy to blow past the context limit.

2.Model performance tends to degrade beyond a certain context length, even if the window technically supports it.

3.Long inputs are expensive, even with prefix caching. You're still paying to transmit and prefill every token.

To deal with this, many agent systems implement context truncation or compression strategies. But overly aggressive compression inevitably leads to information loss. The problem is fundamental: an agent, by nature, must predict the next action based on all prior state—and you can't reliably predict which observation might become critical ten steps later. From a logical standpoint, any irreversible compression carries risk.

That's why we treat the file system as the ultimate context in Manus: unlimited in size, persistent by nature, and directly operable by the agent itself. The model learns to write to and read from files on demand—using the file system not just as storage, but as structured, externalized memory.

Our compression strategies are always designed to be restorable. For instance, the content of a web page can be dropped from the context as long as the URL is preserved, and a document's contents can be omitted if its path remains available in the sandbox. This allows Manus to shrink context length without permanently losing information.

### Keep the Wrong Stuff In

Agents make mistakes. That's not a bug—it's reality. Language models hallucinate, environments return errors, external tools misbehave, and unexpected edge cases show up all the time. In multi-step tasks, failure is not the exception; it's part of the loop.

And yet, a common impulse is to hide these errors: clean up the trace, retry the action, or reset the model's state and leave it to the magical " temperature". That feels safer, more controlled. But it comes at a cost: Erasing failure removes evidence. And without evidence, the model can't adapt.

In our experience, one of the most effective ways to improve agent behavior is deceptively simple: leave the wrong turns in the context. When the model sees a failed action—and the resulting observation or stack trace—it implicitly updates its internal beliefs. This shifts its prior away from similar actions, reducing the chance of repeating the same mistake.

Summary: 
Manus AI employs several specific context engineering techniques to save tokens and manage long contexts. To maximize efficiency, they prioritize a high KV-cache hit rate by keeping the prompt prefix stable (avoiding dynamic timestamps) and ensuring all context is append-only. For managing a large action space without invalidating the cache, they mask token logits instead of dynamically removing tools from the context. To handle contexts that exceed the model's token limit, they use the file system as an 'unlimited' external memory, compressing context by dropping raw data but preserving essential pointers like URLs or file paths. Finally, they intentionally keep failed actions and errors in the context to provide learning evidence for the agent.

### 💾 6. TOKEN SAVER / CONTEXT ENGINEER (Optimización de Recursos y Contexto) – Acciones 701 a 850
*Enfoque: Aplicar las técnicas específicas de Manus AI para reducir costos, optimizar el KV-cache y gestionar ventanas de contexto [[26]], [[28]].*
701. Implementar "Offloading": resumir respuestas de herramientas y almacenar datos completos en archivos externos con punteros, evitando saturar el contexto [[28]].
702. Mantener el prefijo del prompt estable (sin timestamps dinámicos ni variables cambiantes al inicio) para maximizar el KV-cache hit rate y ahorrar hasta 10x en costos [[26]].
703. Asegurar que el contexto sea estrictamente "append-only" (solo adición) para no invalidar la caché de prefijos en iteraciones [[26]].
704. Usar serialización determinista de JSON (orden de claves estable) para evitar diferencias de un solo token que rompan la caché [[26]].
705. Utilizar el sistema de archivos del sandbox como "memoria externa ilimitada", guardando datos allí en lugar de en el prompt [[26]].
706. Aplicar compresión de contexto "restaurable": eliminar contenido web crudo del contexto pero preservar la URL para recuperación bajo demanda [[26]].
707. Enmascarar (mask) logits de herramientas no disponibles en lugar de eliminarlas dinámicamente del prompt, evitando invalidar el KV-cache [[26]].
708. Dejar intencionalmente los errores y stack traces en el contexto para que el agente aprenda y no repita el mismo fallo [[26]].
709. Marcar puntos de quiebre de caché (cache breakpoints) explícitamente después del prompt del sistema si el framework lo requiere [[26]].
710. Reemplazar textos largos de documentación por enlaces o referencias a archivos locales en el entorno de Manus.
711. Solicitar salidas en formato JSON minificado en lugar de texto narrativo para reducir tokens de salida.
712. Dividir tareas masivas en micro-tareas secuenciales para evitar alcanzar el límite máximo de tokens de entrada.
713. Usar IDs de sesión para enrutar solicitudes consistentemente a los mismos trabajadores distribuidos y aprovechar la caché local.
714. Resumir historiales de chat antiguos en un "estado actual" compacto antes de iniciar una nueva rama de conversación.
715. Eliminar metadatos, espacios en blanco excesivos y comentarios innecesarios del código antes de pasarlo al contexto.
716. Configurar al agente para que solicite aclaraciones específicas en lugar de asumir y generar texto de relleno (hallucinaciones).
717. Analizar el uso de tokens por tarea para identificar y eliminar cuellos de botella en el flujo de trabajo del agente.
718. Usar abreviaturas o códigos estandarizados internos para conceptos repetitivos en lugar de descripciones largas.
719. Cargar herramientas (MCP) solo cuando sea estrictamente necesario, pero manteniendo su definición en el contexto (enmascarada) [[26]].
720. Priorizar la recuperación de información (RAG) desde una base de datos vectorial local en lugar de inyectar todo el texto en el prompt.
721. Comprimir imágenes a descripciones textuales concisas antes de pasarlas a modelos de visión, si la resolución no es crítica.
722. Usar variables de entorno para almacenar configuraciones largas en lugar de incluirlas en el prompt del sistema.
723. Agrupar múltiples consultas de API en una sola llamada para reducir la sobrecarga de tokens de herramientas.
724. Descartar observaciones de herramientas que no sean relevantes para el paso actual del razonamiento del agente.
725. Implementar un sistema de "ventana deslizante" que solo mantenga los últimos N pasos de razonamiento en el contexto activo.
726. Usar formatos de datos binarios o codificados (ej. base64 para archivos pequeños) solo cuando sea necesario, prefiriendo referencias.
727. Evitar la repetición de instrucciones de sistema en cada iteración; confiar en la persistencia del contexto inicial.
728. Resumir listas largas de elementos en categorías o rangos (ej. "150 elementos de tipo A" en lugar de listarlos).
729. Usar plantillas de respuesta predefinidas que el agente solo necesita completar con variables, en lugar de generar desde cero.
730. Desactivar la generación de explicaciones verbales ("Aquí está el código que pediste") y pedir solo el bloque de código.

Evidence in page: 
### Technique 1: Offloading - Summarization and Reference Management

Offloading is the practice of summarizing information and storing full data in external references, allowing the agent to access detailed information only when needed. When an AI agent makes a tool call—for example, querying a database or calling an external API—it receives a response that could be quite large. Rather than dumping the entire response into the context window, offloading involves summarizing the key information and providing a reference that the agent can use to retrieve the full data if necessary.

A practical example of this approach comes from Manus AI, a research organization working on advanced AI agents. When their agent makes a tool call and receives a response, they don’t include the entire response in the context. Instead, they provide a concise summary of the response and store the full tool call result in a file or database with a reference pointer. If the agent later determines that it needs more detailed information from that tool call, it can reference the stored data without consuming additional context tokens in the main conversation. This approach mirrors how humans work—we don’t memorize every detail of every conversation, but we keep notes and references we can consult when needed.

Summary: 
According to the article, Manus AI uses a technique called 'offloading' to manage context and save tokens. When their agent receives a large response from a tool call (e.g., a database query), they do not include the entire response in the main conversation's context window. Instead, they summarize the key information for the agent and store the full data in an external reference, such as a file or database. The agent is then provided with a pointer or reference to this stored data, which it can access if it needs more detailed information later. This method allows the agent to function with a leaner, high-signal context while still having access to complete data when necessary.

Evidence in page: 
### Design Around the KV-Cache

If I had to choose just one metric, I'd argue that the KV-cache hit rate is the single most important metric for a production-stage AI agent. It directly affects both latency and cost. To understand why, let's look at how a typical agent operates:

After receiving a user input, the agent proceeds through a chain of tool uses to complete the task. In each iteration, the model selects an action from a predefined action space based on the current context. That action is then executed in the environment (e.g., Manus's virtual machine sandbox) to produce an observation. The action and observation are appended to the context, forming the input for the next iteration. This loop continues until the task is complete.

As you can imagine, the context grows with every step, while the output—usually a structured function call—remains relatively short. This makes the ratio between prefilling and decoding highly skewed in agents compared to chatbots. In Manus, for example, the average input-to-output token ratio is around 100:1.

Fortunately, contexts with identical prefixes can take advantage of KV-cache, which drastically reduces time-to-first-token (TTFT) and inference cost—whether you're using a self-hosted model or calling an inference API. And we're not talking about small savings: with Claude Sonnet, for instance, cached input tokens cost 0.30 USD/MTok, while uncached ones cost 3 USD/MTok—a 10x difference.

From a context engineering perspective, improving KV-cache hit rate involves a few key practices:

1.Keep your prompt prefix stable. Due to the autoregressive nature of LLMs, even a single-token difference can invalidate the cache from that token onward. A common mistake is including a timestamp—especially one precise to the second—at the beginning of the system prompt. Sure, it lets the model tell you the current time, but it also kills your cache hit rate.

2.Make your context append-only. Avoid modifying previous actions or observations. Ensure your serialization is deterministic. Many programming languages and libraries don't guarantee stable key ordering when serializing JSON objects, which can silently break the cache.

3.Mark cache breakpoints explicitly when needed. Some model providers or inference frameworks don't support automatic incremental prefix caching, and instead require manual insertion of cache breakpoints in the context. When assigning these, account for potential cache expiration and at minimum, ensure the breakpoint includes the end of the system prompt.

Additionally, if you're self-hosting models using frameworks like vLLM, make sure prefix/prompt caching is enabled, and that you're using techniques like session IDs to route requests consistently across distributed workers.

### Mask, Don't Remove

As your agent takes on more capabilities, its action space naturally grows more complex—in plain terms, the number of tools explodes. The recent popularity of MCP only adds fuel to the fire. If you allow user-configurable tools, trust me: someone will inevitably plug hundreds of mysterious tools into your carefully curated action space. As a result, the model is more likely to select the wrong action or take an inefficient path. In short, your heavily armed agent gets dumber.

A natural reaction is to design a dynamic action space—perhaps loading tools on demand using something RAG-like. We tried that in Manus too. But our experiments suggest a clear rule: unless absolutely necessary, avoid dynamically adding or removing tools mid-iteration. There are two main reasons for this:

1.In most LLMs, tool definitions live near the front of the context after serialization, typically before or after the system prompt. So any change will invalidate the KV-cache for all subsequent actions and observations.

2.When previous actions and observations still refer to tools that are no longer defined in the current context, the model gets confused. Without constrained decoding, this often leads to schema violations or hallucinated actions.

To solve this while still improving action selection, Manus uses a context-aware state machine to manage tool availability. Rather than removing tools, it masks the token logits during decoding to prevent (or enforce) the selection of certain actions based on the current context.

### Use the File System as Context

Modern frontier LLMs now offer context windows of 128K tokens or more. But in real-world agentic scenarios, that's often not enough, and sometimes even a liability. There are three common pain points:

1.Observations can be huge, especially when agents interact with unstructured data like web pages or PDFs. It's easy to blow past the context limit.

2.Model performance tends to degrade beyond a certain context length, even if the window technically supports it.

3.Long inputs are expensive, even with prefix caching. You're still paying to transmit and prefill every token.

To deal with this, many agent systems implement context truncation or compression strategies. But overly aggressive compression inevitably leads to information loss. The problem is fundamental: an agent, by nature, must predict the next action based on all prior state—and you can't reliably predict which observation might become critical ten steps later. From a logical standpoint, any irreversible compression carries risk.

That's why we treat the file system as the ultimate context in Manus: unlimited in size, persistent by nature, and directly operable by the agent itself. The model learns to write to and read from files on demand—using the file system not just as storage, but as structured, externalized memory.

Our compression strategies are always designed to be restorable. For instance, the content of a web page can be dropped from the context as long as the URL is preserved, and a document's contents can be omitted if its path remains available in the sandbox. This allows Manus to shrink context length without permanently losing information.

### Keep the Wrong Stuff In

Agents make mistakes. That's not a bug—it's reality. Language models hallucinate, environments return errors, external tools misbehave, and unexpected edge cases show up all the time. In multi-step tasks, failure is not the exception; it's part of the loop.

And yet, a common impulse is to hide these errors: clean up the trace, retry the action, or reset the model's state and leave it to the magical " temperature". That feels safer, more controlled. But it comes at a cost: Erasing failure removes evidence. And without evidence, the model can't adapt.

In our experience, one of the most effective ways to improve agent behavior is deceptively simple: leave the wrong turns in the context. When the model sees a failed action—and the resulting observation or stack trace—it implicitly updates its internal beliefs. This shifts its prior away from similar actions, reducing the chance of repeating the same mistake.

Summary: 
Manus AI employs several specific context engineering techniques to save tokens and manage long contexts. To maximize efficiency, they prioritize a high KV-cache hit rate by keeping the prompt prefix stable (avoiding dynamic timestamps) and ensuring all context is append-only. For managing a large action space without invalidating the cache, they mask token logits instead of dynamically removing tools from the context. To handle contexts that exceed the model's token limit, they use the file system as an 'unlimited' external memory, compressing context by dropping raw data but preserving essential pointers like URLs or file paths. Finally, they intentionally keep failed actions and errors in the context to provide learning evidence for the agent.

Basado en la documentación técnica y análisis de capacidades verificadas de **Manus AI** (un agente de IA generalista autónomo diseñado para ejecutar tareas complejas de inicio a fin, con capacidades de construcción de aplicaciones full-stack, generación multimedia e ingeniería de contexto avanzada) [[5]], [[12]], [[26]], a continuación se presenta un compendio masivo, denso y sin relleno de **1000 acciones específicas** agrupadas por los roles solicitados. 

Cada ítem representa un caso de uso práctico, accionable y verificable dentro del ecosistema de Manus AI.

---

### 🧠 1. VIBE CODER (Desarrollo Intuitivo y Autónomo) – Acciones 1 a 150

2. Crear landing pages con diseño responsive, animaciones CSS y formularios funcionales.

### 🎬 3. VIDEO PROMPTER (Dirección y Generación de Video con IA) – Acciones 251 a 400

### 💾 6. TOKEN SAVER / CONTEXT ENGINEER (Optimización de Recursos y Contexto) – Acciones 701 a 850
*Enfoque: Aplicar las técnicas específicas de Manus AI para reducir costos, optimizar el KV-cache y gestionar ventanas de contexto [[26]], [[28]].*
701. Implementar "Offloading": resumir respuestas de herramientas y almacenar datos completos en archivos externos con punteros, evitando saturar el contexto [[28]].
702. Mantener el prefijo del prompt estable (sin timestamps dinámicos ni variables cambiantes al inicio) para maximizar el KV-cache hit rate y ahorrar hasta 10x en costos [[26]].
703. Asegurar que el contexto sea estrictamente "append-only" (solo adición) para no invalidar la caché de prefijos en iteraciones [[26]].
704. Usar serialización determinista de JSON (orden de claves estable) para evitar diferencias de un solo token que rompan la caché [[26]].
705. Utilizar el sistema de archivos del sandbox como "memoria externa ilimitada", guardando datos allí en lugar de en el prompt [[26]].
706. Aplicar compresión de contexto "restaurable": eliminar contenido web crudo del contexto pero preservar la URL para recuperación bajo demanda [[26]].
707. Enmascarar (mask) logits de herramientas no disponibles en lugar de eliminarlas dinámicamente del prompt, evitando invalidar el KV-cache [[26]].
708. Dejar intencionalmente los errores y stack traces en el contexto para que el agente aprenda y no repita el mismo fallo [[26]].
709. Marcar puntos de quiebre de caché (cache breakpoints) explícitamente después del prompt del sistema si el framework lo requiere [[26]].
710. Reemplazar textos largos de documentación por enlaces o referencias a archivos locales en el entorno de Manus.
711. Solicitar salidas en formato JSON minificado en lugar de texto narrativo para reducir tokens de salida.
712. Dividir tareas masivas en micro-tareas secuenciales para evitar alcanzar el límite máximo de tokens de entrada.
713. Usar IDs de sesión para enrutar solicitudes consistentemente a los mismos trabajadores distribuidos y aprovechar la caché local.
714. Resumir historiales de chat antiguos en un "estado actual" compacto antes de iniciar una nueva rama de conversación.
715. Eliminar metadatos, espacios en blanco excesivos y comentarios innecesarios del código antes de pasarlo al contexto.
716. Configurar al agente para que solicite aclaraciones específicas en lugar de asumir y generar texto de relleno (hallucinaciones).
717. Analizar el uso de tokens por tarea para identificar y eliminar cuellos de botella en el flujo de trabajo del agente.
718. Usar abreviaturas o códigos estandarizados internos para conceptos repetitivos en lugar de descripciones largas.
719. Cargar herramientas (MCP) solo cuando sea estrictamente necesario, pero manteniendo su definición en el contexto (enmascarada) [[26]].
720. Priorizar la recuperación de información (RAG) desde una base de datos vectorial local en lugar de inyectar todo el texto en el prompt.
721. Comprimir imágenes a descripciones textuales concisas antes de pasarlas a modelos de visión, si la resolución no es crítica.
722. Usar variables de entorno para almacenar configuraciones largas en lugar de incluirlas en el prompt del sistema.
723. Agrupar múltiples consultas de API en una sola llamada para reducir la sobrecarga de tokens de herramientas.
724. Descartar observaciones de herramientas que no sean relevantes para el paso actual del razonamiento del agente.
725. Implementar un sistema de "ventana deslizante" que solo mantenga los últimos N pasos de razonamiento en el contexto activo.
726. Usar formatos de datos binarios o codificados (ej. base64 para archivos pequeños) solo cuando sea necesario, prefiriendo referencias.
727. Evitar la repetición de instrucciones de sistema en cada iteración; confiar en la persistencia del contexto inicial.
728. Resumir listas largas de elementos en categorías o rangos (ej. "150 elementos de tipo A" en lugar de listarlos).
729. Usar plantillas de respuesta predefinidas que el agente solo necesita completar con variables, en lugar de generar desde cero.
730. Desactivar la generación de explicaciones verbales ("Aquí está el código que pediste") y pedir solo el bloque de código.
731. Consolidar múltiples archivos de configuración pequeños en un solo archivo de referencia para reducir llamadas de lectura.
732. Usar índices o tablas de contenido para navegar documentos largos en lugar de cargar el documento completo.
733. Implementar un mecanismo de "olvido selectivo" donde el agente descarta detalles de pasos ya completados y verificados.
734. Optimizar los nombres de las herramientas y descripciones para que sean concisos pero inequívocos.
735. Evitar el uso de ejemplos de few-shot prompting excesivamente largos; usar uno o dos ejemplos de alta densidad.
736. Usar tipos de datos estrictos en las definiciones de herramientas para evitar que el agente genere entradas inválidas que requieran reintentos (y más tokens).
737. Almacenar resultados intermedios de cálculos complejos en variables o archivos en lugar de recalcularlos o mantenerlos en el historial.
738. Usar comandos de terminal concisos en lugar de scripts largos cuando una sola línea pueda lograr el objetivo.
739. Implementar validación de esquema en el lado del cliente (sandbox) para rechazar respuestas mal formadas antes de que consuman más contexto.
740. Agrupar tareas de lectura de archivos en una sola operación de herramienta en lugar de múltiples lecturas individuales.
741. Usar patrones de diseño de prompts que fomenten la concisión (ej. "Responde en máximo 3 viñetas").
742. Eliminar saludos, despedidas y cortesías del protocolo de comunicación agente-entorno.
743. Usar identificadores cortos (UUIDs cortos o hashes) para referenciar objetos en lugar de descripciones textuales largas.

746. Usar formatos de serialización más compactos (ej. YAML o TOML en lugar de JSON verboso) cuando sea compatible.
747. Descartar automáticamente las salidas de herramientas que excedan un umbral de tokens predefinido, solicitando un resumen en su lugar.
748. Mantener un registro externo de decisiones tomadas para no tener que justificarlas repetidamente en el contexto.
749. Usar referencias cruzadas (ej. "ver paso 3") en lugar de repetir la información de ese paso.
